hints: Focus on what the colorimeter actually measures, absorbance is not concentration, so you will need both graphs together.
Look at the left calibration graph first and find the simple link between absorbance and iodine concentration.
Find the gradient of the tangent to the right-hand curve at 20 s, then convert that absorbance change per second into concentration change per second.
walkthrough:
**Use the calibration curve to link absorbance to concentration**

Think of the left graph as your translator. It turns a colorimeter reading into a real concentration.

From the graph, absorbance 0.5 corresponds to $0.25 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and absorbance 0.1 corresponds to $0.05 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. So:
$$[\text{I}_2] = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \times \text{absorbance}$$

**Find the rate of change of absorbance at 20 s**

Rate at a particular time means the gradient of the tangent at that point, not an average over the whole reaction.

At 20 s, absorbance is 0.30. Drawing a tangent at 20 s on the absorbance-time curve gives a fall of about 0.40 absorbance units over 40 s, from about 0.50 to 0.10:
$$\text{gradient} \approx \frac{\Delta \text{absorbance}}{\Delta t} = \frac{-0.40}{40} = -0.01 \text{ s}^{-1}$$

**Convert absorbance rate to concentration rate**

Now translate that colour change rate into a chemical rate. Ignore the minus sign, rate is positive for disappearance.

$$\text{rate} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.01 = 5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$$

options.A: Correct. A tangent gradient of about 0.01 absorbance units per second multiplied by the calibration factor $0.5 \times 10^{-3}$ gives $5 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \text{ s}^{-1}$.
options.B: Too large by a factor of 2. This comes from misreading the calibration slope, for example using $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ per absorbance unit instead of $0.5 \times 10^{-3}$, or from a steeper tangent estimate.
options.C: Too large by 1000 times. This is the classic trap of forgetting the $\times 10^{-3}$ on the concentration axis of the calibration curve and treating 0.25 as $0.25 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
options.D: Far too large. This combines forgetting the $10^{-3}$ factor with overestimating the gradient, for example dividing absorbance change by too short a time interval.
